name: Kojic acid
lead: Kojic acid is a compound made by several fungi, notably Aspergillus oryzae, the koji mold of Japanese cooking, and it forms as a by-product when rice is fermented for sake. [1][21] In skin care it is used to fade dark spots and uneven tone: it appears in soaps, cleansers, creams and serums aimed at melasma, post-acne marks and sun spots, and users apply it to even out complexion for a clearer, more uniform look. [1][2][3][4]

It works by inhibiting tyrosinase, the copper-containing enzyme that starts melanin synthesis, and by chelating copper at the enzyme's active site. [2][22] Reviews list it among conventional topical agents for hyperpigmentation alongside hydroquinone and glycolic acid, and as an adjuvant in melasma regimens. [3][4][5] Hydroquinone and triple-combination creams remain the best-studied agents. [3]

Human trial evidence consists mostly of small, short studies, often of kojic acid inside combination products. [6] A 60-patient Indian study found 4 percent hydroquinone acted faster than a 0.75 percent kojic acid cream that also contained vitamin C. [5] In the European Union a 2024 regulation allows kojic acid in cosmetics only in face and hand products at up to 1 percent, applying to products placed on the market from 1 November 2025. [1] Wikipedia's skin-whitening article lists redness and eczema among its side effects. [23]

paras: Kojic acid is used to lighten melasma and other pigmentation and appears in cleansers, soaps, creams and serums, sometimes with turmeric extracts or vitamin C.[1][5][7] A US over-the-counter listing for a turmeric kojic acid facial cleanser describes its use as cleansing facial skin only.[7]

It is most often used for melasma, a chronic and relapsing patchy hyperpigmentation of the face that is triggered by ultraviolet exposure, hormones and genetics and is more common in women and people with darker skin types. [24] Wikipedia lists topical kojic acid (at 2 percent) among melasma options alongside hydroquinone, azelaic acid, tretinoin, cysteamine and alpha arbutin, plus oral tranexamic acid, peels and lasers, and notes that strict sun protection and sunscreens with physical blockers are preferred. [24] Sources on hyperpigmentation also list post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation after acne and solar lentigines as targets. [25][11]

Kojic acid is used on cut fruit to limit browning, in seafood to preserve color, as an antibacterial and antifungal agent, and as a precursor to the flavorant maltol.[1] Reviews describe pharmaceutical research on derivatives with antimicrobial, antioxidant and other properties.[2]

Reviews of melasma treatment describe hydroquinone and triple combination creams as the best-studied topical agents, with kojic acid among alternatives and combination partners.[3][4][8] A 2013 prospective study in 60 patients with facial melasma compared nightly 4 percent hydroquinone with 0.75 percent kojic acid plus 2.5 percent vitamin C: kojic acid showed no significant MASI change at week 4 and significant decreases at weeks 8 and 12, while hydroquinone improved significantly from week 4, and the authors reported hydroquinone as superior at each time point.[5] The study had no placebo control and a short 12-week follow-up, and vitamin C in the kojic acid arm limits attribution.[5]

A 2025 split-face pilot tested a cosmetic with 5 percent alpha-arbutin and 2 percent kojic acid against triple combination cream, and other studies tested kojic acid inside combination products.[9] Research with human tyrosinase has noted that many inhibitors identified with mushroom tyrosinase lack clinical efficacy.[10]

A 2022 systematic review of topical melasma treatments analysed 80 papers and reported that triple-combination therapy and hydroquinone are the most studied agents, and that ascorbic acid, azelaic acid, glycolic acid, kojic acid, salicylic acid and niacinamide have been shown effective as adjuvant therapies with minimal side effects. [3] A 2018 study screened 50,000 compounds against recombinant human tyrosinase and compared hits with established whitening agents, reporting that most inhibitors found using mushroom tyrosinase lack clinical efficacy. [10] A 1994 kinetics paper described kojic acid as a slow-binding inhibitor of tyrosinase's catecholase activity. [26]

Human studies include the 60-patient comparison with hydroquinone,[5] a randomized comparison of treatments in solar lentigines of Asian women,[11] a study of actinic lentigines under bleaching treatment,[12] comparisons of melasma modalities and chemical peels,[13][14] and a split-face pilot with alpha-arbutin plus kojic acid.[9] Reviews and consensus include a 2026 Pigmentary Disorders Society Delphi consensus with 38 dermatologists,[15] and reviews of topical melasma therapy, multimodal management and kojic acid applications.[2][3][4][8]
A registered trial of a peeling product for melasma (n=10) and trials of herbal creams and adjuvant programs are listed.[16][17][18]

Reviews describe contact dermatitis and irritation as the main concerns and note that kojic acid is unstable in light and air.[2] Wikipedia states that kojic acid may be weakly carcinogenic according to some animal studies, is not believed to reach carcinogenic thresholds in human skin and is considered safe at cosmetic levels, while the EU has restricted its cosmetic concentration to 1 percent in face and hand products.[1] In the hydroquinone comparison, mild erythema or burning was reported in a small number of patients in each arm, although the paper's results and discussion differ on the figures.[5]

Wikipedia's article on skin whitening lists redness and eczema as side effects of kojic acid and notes that hydroquinone, a commonly compared agent, is linked to ochronosis and carries unresolved cancer-risk questions; the same article notes that the EU banned hydroquinone in cosmetics in 2000. [23] Wikipedia's hydroquinone article says the US FDA banned over-the-counter hydroquinone products in 2020. [27] A 2020 paper describing a newer lightening compound said many preparations containing hydroquinone, kojic acid, arbutin and deoxyarbutin are toxic to melanocytes in lab assays. [28]

Kojic acid inhibits tyrosinase, the enzyme that starts melanin synthesis, and chelates copper at its active site; it also has antioxidant activity.[2] Kojate, the deprotonated form, binds ferric iron to give a red complex, which may reflect its biological role in solubilizing iron.[1]

The compound has the formula HOCH2C5H2O2OH (5-hydroxy-2-hydroxymethyl-4H-pyran-4-one). Labelling studies indicate at least two biosynthetic routes, mainly via dehydration of glucose; industrial production relies on aerobic fermentation.[1]

Kojic acid is named for koji, the Japanese word for Aspergillus oryzae. Wikipedia's article on the mold describes its use in sake, miso and soy sauce, notes that scholars disagree on whether China or Japan first used it in fermentation, and says the Brewing Society of Japan approved calling it the national fungus in 2006. [21] That article reports that A. oryzae has not been found to produce aflatoxins, although it is closely related to species that do. [21]

Grokipedia, an AI-generated source that should be treated with caution, states that kojic acid was isolated in 1907 by Kendo Saito from Aspergillus oryzae and named by Teijiro Yabuta in 1912. [19] Wikipedia cites a 1924 paper by Yabuta on its structure and a 2006 review tracing a century of research from Japanese foods to cosmetics. [1] A 1956 chemistry review covers early work on the compound. [20]

Kojic acid moved from food fermentation into skin care as a tyrosinase inhibitor, and by the 1990s it was described in the literature as a cosmetic skin-whitening agent. [26] The most recent regulatory step is the 2024 EU regulation (Commission Regulation (EU) 2024/996) that added it to Annex III of the Cosmetics Regulation, permitting it only in face and hand products at up to 1 percent from 1 November 2025. [1]

Wikipedia's skin-whitening article describes a large global market for lightening products driven by cultural associations of lighter skin with beauty and status, reports survey figures such as 77 percent of Nigerian women using lightening products in 2013, and notes that many agents are restricted or banned in various countries. [23] It lists kojic acid as an agent found effective in some studies and allowed in cosmetics. [23]
In the US a turmeric kojic acid facial cleanser is listed on DailyMed with a label describing it as a facial cleanser. [7]

In appearance forums kojic acid soaps appear in discussions of skin tone. One looksmax.org member posted about receiving a glutathione, lycopene and kojic acid soap, saying their skin colour was fine but that they preferred a redder undertone to a yellower one, and a reply asked which brand. [29] Such use is for overall tone, whereas the published trials concern localised pigmentation such as melasma and lentigines. [5][9][11]

lore.intro: Kojic acid is discussed in appearance communities mainly through soaps and tone-evening products, and in dermatology as one of several tyrosinase inhibitors used for pigmentation. [29][3]

claims.claim: Kojic acid soap evens out or changes overall skin tone.
claims.believers: A looksmax.org member wrote about getting a glutathione, lycopene and kojic acid soap while aiming for a redder undertone. [29]
claims.experts: Published trials study localised pigmentation such as melasma and lentigines, and no study found examines kojic acid soap for overall skin tone. [5][11]

claims.claim: Kojic acid fades melasma and dark spots.
claims.believers: Products and reviews position it as a standard brightening ingredient used alone or with vitamin C or turmeric. [1][7]
claims.experts: A 2013 trial found 0.75 percent kojic acid plus vitamin C reduced MASI scores at weeks 8 and 12 but acted more slowly than 4 percent hydroquinone. [5]

claims.claim: Kojic acid is a safer natural alternative to hydroquinone.
claims.believers: It comes from fermentation fungi and is marketed as a gentler option after hydroquinone restrictions. [1][23]
claims.experts: Wikipedia reports it may be weakly carcinogenic in some animal studies but considered safe at cosmetic levels, and the EU now caps it at 1 percent in face and hand products. [1]

claims.claim: Any tyrosinase inhibitor that works on mushrooms will work on skin.
claims.believers: Lab screening with mushroom tyrosinase has identified many candidate whitening ingredients. [26]
claims.experts: A 2018 study reported that most inhibitors found with mushroom tyrosinase lack clinical efficacy against the human enzyme. [10]

claims.claim: Kojic acid products can irritate skin.
claims.believers: Forum users generally discuss it for soaps and cleansers that rinse off. [29]
claims.experts: Reviews describe contact dermatitis and irritation as the main concerns and note the compound is unstable in light and air; Wikipedia lists redness and eczema. [2][23]

Inhibits tyrosinase, the enzyme that starts melanin production
Less new pigment forms in dark patches
Spots and melasma look lighter and tone looks more even
angle.text: Kojic acid is used on the skin to lighten dark patches such as melasma, sun spots and post-acne marks, giving a more even complexion. It acts on pigment production rather than removing a skin layer, so results build up over weeks to months in studies.
